title: FLINT: Coupling Proximal Initialization and Bounded Stochasticity for Flow-Matching Inverse Problems
claim: Existing methods either correct trajectories from random noise or optimize the source noise; coupling a good start with bounded stochasticity reaches the target reliably.
layout: 5 panels left-to-right, four prior grouped by space, ours highlighted at right
description: Five side-by-side schematic panels share the same geometry. Each shows nested curved manifolds M_1 down to M_0, a green slanted line for the measurement constraint y = Ax, and arrows for the sampling path. Panels (a) and (b) sit under a 'Trajectory space methods' header. They show blue score steps with red likelihood-correction arrows starting from random initialization. Panels (c) and (d) sit under 'Source space methods'. They show red arrows or wiggly red curves moving along the top manifold, then one long blue arrow down to x_0. Panel (e), set off by a dashed vertical line, is labeled FLINT (Ours). It has a red proximal source initialization wiggle, then a dark blue path inside a light-blue tube labeled 'Bounded Stochasticity'. The path ends at a red star on the constraint line. Method names appear under each panel.
caption: Illustration of generative paradigms for inverse problems. (a) and (b) depict trajectoryspace methods, while panels (c) and (d) depict source-space optimization methods. (a) Likelihood score corrections are applied directly at each noisy intermediate state xt. (b) Likelihood score corrections are applied in clean image space via the Tweedie estimate ˆx0|t, followed by renoising to the generative manifold at the next timestep. (c) Source-space MAP methods reparameterize the clean image via the deterministic generative map Φ as x0 = Φ(x1) and optimize over the initial noise x1 to minimize data fidelity. (d) Source-space posterior sampling draws samples from p(x1 | y) via Hamiltonian Monte Carlo or Langevin dynamics. (e) By strategically coupling proximal source initialization with bounded stochasticity during guided posterior sampling, FLINT bounds the sampling trajectory, preserving the initialization advantage and yielding high-fidelity convergence.
abstract: Flow matching models have emerged as a dominant paradigm for generative posterior sampling in imaging inverse problems. Existing solvers follow two distinct lines of work: trajectory-space methods, which refine sampling dynamics from random initial noise, and source-space methods, which optimize the initial noise itself. While most prior work treats these as independent design choices, we show that they are inherently coupled. We derive a unified stability bound that links initialization proximity and cumulative sampling stochasticity through a multiplicative envelope, complemented by two empirical observations. First, we identify a sufficiency regime in which a moderately optimized proximal source initialization is enough to attain the performance plateau, rendering exhaustive source-space optimization unnecessary. Second, this initial advantage is fragile: it is eroded by excessive stochasticity accumulation during guided sampling, necessitating a mechanism that bounds the cumulative noise injection. These findings motivate FLINT, a two-stage framework that operationalizes this coupling. FLINT establishes a high-fidelity starting point via a manifold-constrained proximal objective in only a few iterations, then performs guided sampling under a bounded stochasticity schedule that helps prevent erasure of the initialization advantage. Across diverse inverse problems, FLINT delivers state of the art perceptual quality and competitive distortion metrics while maintaining superior computational efficiency.
